title: Suncorp profit down, but investors rewarded
full_text:
Insurer Suncorp blamed catastrophic weather for an $800m earnings hit sweetened by a special dividend and buying back $250m of its own shares.
The Queensland-based company also dumped consulting firm KPMG as its auditor and switched to EY Oceania, which will take over its 2027 audit. Suncorp chief executive Steve Johnston said the decision was taken to exit the 30-year relationship with KPMG before the scandal surrounding the firm’s audit breaches erupted.
Suncorp’s profit for the year ended June 30 was down sharply from $1.8bn last year. It came amid a $254m overrun in Suncorp’s natural hazard losses, which are claims paid by the insurer for wild weather and storms. It paid $10.02bn in claims, up from $9.25bn. Cash profit was $1.04bn. Suncorp paid $2.02bn in natural hazard claims, after only budgeting $1.77bn. The insurer had secured additional reinsurance cover aimed at “significantly reducing natural hazard risk and earnings volatility”. Suncorp’s gross written premium rose 2.7 per cent to $15.4bn. It expects to increase premiums by 3-5 per cent in the year ahead.
Suncorp sold its banking arm to ANZ for $4.9bn in 2024, simplifying itself as a general insurance, commercial and New Zealand operation. “The aggregate cover is an important component for Suncorp post the bank sale, significantly reducing natural hazard risk and earnings volatility,” Mr Johnston said. The insurer declared a 52c-a-share dividend, plus a 10c special dividend, joining its 17c interim dividend. In addition, Suncorp will run a $250m buyback, after already buying back $400m of its shares over the 2026 financial year. The stock rose 3.3 per cent to $19.18.
